thread.title: Why the markets should ignore Trump - MarketWatch

author: Tim Mullaney
title: Why the markets should ignore Trump - MarketWatch
text:
NICHOLAS KAMM/AFP/Getty Images President Donald Trump speaks at the American Center for Mobility in Ypsilanti, Mich., with General Motors CEO Mary Barra and other auto industry executives on March 15, 2017. Here we go again: The president of the United States has his iPhone out, and wants to tweet about stocks and markets. He’s slappin’ tariffs on Apple, yankin’ subsidies from General Motors, and smackin’ down the Federal Reserve chair he himself appointed last year, all while claiming that the falling price of oil is, implicitly, showing the wisdom of Donald Trump looking the other way after Saudi Arabia murdered journalist Jamal Khashoggi.
If only that were how this worked. But it’s not how any of this works.
Of all the topics on which Trump’s ignorance is truly boundless, his lack of knowledge of the markets is complemented here by the fact that he doesn’t know even the Schoolhouse Rock Jr. version of how a bill becomes law under the Constitution.
That’s why market moves — the drop in Apple AAPL, +0.97% shares on reports that Trump wants to impose tariffs on Chinese-assembled iPhones in January, and the dip in General Motors GM, -1.53% on Tuesday (after a Monday surge) after Trump tweeted that he would remove federal subsidies for GM electric cars — are both a tad misplaced.
And it goes almost without saying that everyone should blow off Trump’s criticism of Fed Chair Jerome Powell, whom the Washington Post reported last night got his job partly because Trump thought Janet Yellen was too short to run the central bank for another term. The Fed will ignore the president, and certainly should.
Trump the stock picker is a topic we’ve had fun with before.
Back in January 2017, we celebrated the inauguration by looking at 37 companies about which Trump had tweeted investment advice. As we would learn, Trump’s tweets reflect his personal preferences — his view of Facebook’s FB, -1.98% IPO was colored by his opinion on CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s decision to get married without a prenuptial agreement, and so on.
From the Archives: Trading on Trump’s tweets would have left you sad and poorer
By our math, he prospectively lost investors money about 80% of the time — he disliked companies about to make a mint, notably the “failing New York Times,” NYT, +1.67% and liked several that were headed for trouble.
But this week, he’s talking about some of the best-known names in the market, and since he’s president now there’s more chance his words might have consequences. So let’s review — GM first, since it’s the easiest one.
The big subsidy GM gets for electric cars, along with every other car maker, is that its customers can claim a $7,500 federal tax credit. That subsidy costs about $400 million a year for all auto makers, a pittance next to GM’s $145 billion in 2017 sales. It also phases out after to the first 200,000 electric vehicles each auto maker sells, a target GM expects to hit by next year.
After that, no subsidies — even though Congress could and should extend them to fight climate change.
So Trump’s threat is as empty as his head.
Stopping there wouldn’t do justice to the president’s dunderheadedness this week, though. Riddle yourself this: How does tax law get changed? Oh yeah, it requires action by Congress, and middle-schoolers are taught that a little document called the Constitution specifies that tax legislation originate in the House of Representatives.
The same House that will be controlled by the opposition party in January, because Trump’s party lost about 40 seats in this month’s election.
Let’s say GM will be fine. Just as it was when Trump tweeted on them in late 2016 — right before a 50% rally that ended when Trump’s tariffs on aluminum and steel raised GM’s annual costs by $1 billion. I’ll even wager GM finds an SUV to make in the plant in Youngstown, Ohio, it moved this week toward closing, replacing Chevy Cruze sedans that are out of favor thanks to low gas prices.
They may even let Trump claim credit when they do.
Apple’s a slightly tougher case, since Trump does have authority to impose tariffs, if he wants, to get leverage on China in trade talks. In theory those tariffs could raise iPhone prices when unit sales are already slowing, hurting Apple for a spell. But Trump’s policies won’t outlast what’s probably waiting for him in 2020 at the polls, if they even get imposed in the first place.
After all, if we know anything about Trump it’s that he’s unusually a creature of self-interest, and his self-interest would be ill-served by an up-to-25% jump in the cost of everything American consumers import from China — beginning with iPhones.
Oil CLF9, -0.97% isn’t falling because Trump shined the Saudis’ shoes, either — it’s falling because Trump’s sanctions on Iran have turned out to be riddled with loopholes that have kept Iran’s crude flowing to China and India, who were Iran’s biggest customers anyway.
And apparently Trump didn’t tell the Saudis that until right before sanctions took effect Nov. 4, after Riyadh raised production to offset Iranian crude leaving the world market. So Saudi Arabia is selling its crude for much less than it expected.
Whoops.
That’s not how you treat your friends, Mr. President. Especially when you’re short on pals already.
Especially friends with bone saws.
